channel.title: Kaho's Ibaraki Blog
channel.description: Stories about Ibaraki, Japan by Kaho, a local: places, food, travel tips and real life in rural Japan.

item.title: Coming to Mito Station? Buy this ¥699 sushi bowl
item.description: Coming to Mito Station in Ibaraki? Grab a supermarket chirashi sushi bowl with tuna, salmon, crab and tobiko for ¥699 (¥754 with tax). Cheap, fresh and tasty.

item.title: I feel better! Homemade karaage after a 1-hour walk
item.description: Feeling better after a fever, I walked for an hour in Mito and made homemade karaage, crispy Japanese fried chicken coated in potato starch.

item.title: Japan’s Thanksgiving has no turkey: Kinro Kansha no Hi
item.description: Kinro Kansha no Hi, Japan’s Labor Thanksgiving Day on November 23: its roots in the Niinamesai rice harvest festival, how people celebrate it, and tips for visitors.

item.title: Ibaraki-ben: a fun guide to the Ibaraki dialect
item.description: A friendly guide to the Ibaraki dialect (Ibaraki-ben): why it sounds flat, the famous “-ppe” ending, and words like gojappe, aonajimi and shaanme.

item.title: Momiji-dera: the hidden maple temple in Daigo, Ibaraki
item.description: Eigenji, the “Maple Temple” in Daigo, Ibaraki: red maples on a hill, a view over the town, when the leaves peak, free entry and how to get there from Tokyo.

item.title: Iwaki La La Mew: a $19 seafood bowl by the sea in Fukushima
item.description: Iwaki La La Mew at Onahama Port, Fukushima: huge seafood bowls, a fresh fish market, seafood BBQ, opening hours and how to get there from Ibaraki and Tokyo.

item.title: My real morning in rural Japan: no fancy life
item.description: A real weekday morning of a Japanese office worker in the Ibaraki countryside: waking at 6am, skincare, homemade onigiri, breakfast by the water and a quiet walk.

item.title: No trash cans in Japan? Where the garbage goes
item.description: Why Japan has so few public trash cans, why the streets are still clean, how garbage sorting and collection days work in towns like Ibaraki, and tips for visitors.

item.title: Kairakuen in autumn: Mito’s maple valley in Ibaraki
item.description: Kairakuen in Mito, Ibaraki is one of Japan’s three great gardens. In autumn, visit Momijidani maple valley, the bamboo and cedar woods, and Kobuntei.

item.title: Kuuki wo yomu: the Japanese art of “reading the air”
item.description: Kuuki wo yomu (空気を読む) means “reading the air” in Japan: what it is, the word KY, why Japan works this way, how it feels in the countryside, and easy tips for visitors.

item.title: Kashima Jingu: Ibaraki’s ancient shrine in the forest
item.description: Kashima Jingu in Ibaraki is one of Kanto’s oldest shrines: a red tower gate, sacred deer, a cedar forest, the earthquake stone and easy access from Tokyo.

item.title: A Japanese supermarket in Ibaraki: ¥357 bento and lots of sushi
item.description: A walk through a local supermarket in rural Ibaraki, Japan: ¥357 karaage and tonkatsu bento, packs of sushi, sweet winter mikan, bakery bread and tips for visitors.

item.title: Kairo: Japan’s little pocket heaters for winter
item.description: What kairo are, why Japan loves these disposable heat packs in winter, the history from warm stones to Hokaron, the stick-on and shoe types, and how to use them safely.

item.title: Hananuki Gorge: Ibaraki’s red bridge of autumn leaves
item.description: Hananuki Gorge in Takahagi, Ibaraki: when the autumn leaves peak, the 60m Shiomi Falls suspension bridge, the 2026 festival and light-up, and how to get there.

item.title: Yesterday and this morning: apples, leaves, cake and the gym
item.description: A real two-day diary from Ibaraki: apple picking and autumn leaves in Daigo, a big birthday dinner for my dad, then a 6am gym and the best protein shake.

item.title: Bonenkai: Japan’s “forget the year” party
item.description: What a bonenkai is, why Japanese companies and friends hold forget-the-year parties in December, drinking manners like kanpai and pouring for others, and tips for visitors.

item.title: Okukuji apples: apple picking in Daigo, Ibaraki
item.description: Apple picking in Daigo, Ibaraki: what Okukuji apples are, when the season ends, orchards like Himegataki, an apple bath onsen, and how to get there.

item.title: Why rural Japan is full of rice fields
item.description: Why the Japanese countryside is full of rice paddies: what gohan really means, the rice year in Ibaraki, shinmai new rice, Labor Thanksgiving Day, and tips for visitors.

item.title: Oarai Isosaki Shrine: Ibaraki’s torii in the sea
item.description: Oarai Isosaki Shrine in Ibaraki has a torii on the rocks in the Pacific. Its legend, when to see the sunrise, safety tips and how to get there.

item.title: A weekend from Ibaraki: swans at Lake Inawashiro and a wine harvest festival
item.description: A weekend drive from Ibaraki: a clear morning with swans and Mt. Bandai at Lake Inawashiro in Fukushima, then a wine harvest festival in Tochigi.

item.title: No tipping in Japan: why the staff may run after you with your change
item.description: Why there is no tipping in Japan, why staff may run after you with your change, service charges, ryokan envelopes, and simple ways to say thank you.

item.title: Ibaraki lotus root: Japan’s renkon capital at Kasumigaura
item.description: Ibaraki grows about half of Japan’s lotus root (renkon) around Lake Kasumigaura. When it’s in season, how it’s harvested, and easy ways to eat it.

item.title: Sumimasen: the Japanese word for sorry, thank you and excuse me
item.description: Why Japanese people say sumimasen (すみません) for sorry, thank you and excuse me, where the word comes from, and simple tips for using it in Japan.

item.title: Ryujin Suspension Bridge: Ibaraki’s dragon gorge in autumn
item.description: Ryujin Suspension Bridge in Ibaraki is a 375m walking bridge 100m above a dragon-shaped gorge. Autumn leaves festival, fees, bungee and how to get there.

item.title: Hitachi Station: the glass train station over the ocean
item.description: Hitachi Station in Ibaraki is a glass station that looks out over the Pacific. Who designed it, the Sea Birds Cafe, and tips for visiting from Tokyo.

item.title: Mito natto: why Ibaraki is Japan’s natto capital
item.description: Why Mito in Ibaraki is Japan’s natto city: the samurai legend, why the beans are small, straw-wrapped wara natto, soboro natto, and how to eat it.

item.title: Shoes off in Japan: the genkan, the step, and the toilet slippers
item.description: Why Japanese people take off their shoes at the genkan, the small step that marks inside and outside, the slipper and toilet slipper rules, and easy tips for visitors.

item.title: Ushiku Daibutsu: Ibaraki’s giant 120m Buddha
item.description: Ushiku Daibutsu in Ibaraki is a 120m bronze Buddha you can go inside. What to see, the 85m view, seasons and how to get there from Tokyo.

item.title: Eating while walking in Japan: rude or not?
item.description: Is it rude to eat while walking in Japan? What tabearuki means, why many Japanese people stop to eat, the big exceptions like festivals and food streets, and simple tips for visitors.

item.title: Mount Tsukuba autumn leaves: Ibaraki’s easy day trip from Tokyo
item.description: Mount Tsukuba in Ibaraki is a 45-minute train ride from Akihabara. When the autumn leaves peak, the free evening light-up, and how to get there.

item.title: Chopstick manners in Japan: the rules nobody tells you
item.description: Japanese chopstick manners explained simply: why you never stand chopsticks in rice or pass food chopstick to chopstick, the other small rules, and easy tips for visitors.

item.title: Ankou nabe: Ibaraki’s winter anglerfish hot pot
item.description: Ankou nabe is Ibaraki’s famous winter anglerfish hot pot. When it is in season, the “seven tools,” the hanging cut, dobujiru and where to try it.

item.title: Ohitorisama: why eating alone in Japan is totally normal
item.description: What ohitorisama means, why eating alone in Japan is normal and not sad, the restaurants made for one person, and easy tips for solo travelers, with an Ibaraki example.

item.title: Oiwa Shrine: I went to Ibaraki’s most famous power spot
item.description: A local’s visit to Oiwa Shrine in Hitachi, Ibaraki: why it is a famous power spot, the 188 gods, the Three Cedars, the mountain trail, and how to get there.

item.title: Otoshi: the izakaya dish you didn’t order (and why you pay for it)
item.description: Why Japanese izakaya bring a small dish you did not order and add it to the bill: what otoshi (tsukidashi) is, typical price, why it exists, and tips for visitors.

item.title: Shichi-Go-San: why tiny kimono fill Japan’s shrines in November
item.description: What Shichi-Go-San (November 15) is, why Japan celebrates kids aged 3, 5 and 7, the long chitose-ame candy, how families celebrate in Ibaraki, and tips for visitors.

item.title: Omiyage: why Japanese people bring snacks back to the office
item.description: What omiyage is, why Japanese people bring snacks to the office after a trip, the unwritten rules, and classic Ibaraki omiyage like Mito no Ume and hoshiimo.

item.title: Kasama Chrysanthemum Festival: Ibaraki’s flower shrine
item.description: Kasama Chrysanthemum Festival at Kasama Inari Shrine, Ibaraki: 2026 dates (Oct 24–Nov 23), chrysanthemum dolls, free entry, events and how to get there.

item.title: Why Japanese houses are so cold in winter
item.description: Why many Japanese homes have no central heating, how the kotatsu heated table works, the heat shock risk in cold bathrooms, and winter tips for visitors.

item.title: Fukuroda Falls in autumn: a giant waterfall and red leaves
item.description: Fukuroda Falls in Ibaraki is one of Japan's three great waterfalls. When to see the autumn leaves, tickets, hours, the light-up and how to get there from Tokyo.

item.title: Raw egg on rice? Why Japan eats TKG for breakfast
item.description: Tamago kake gohan (TKG) is raw egg on hot rice, a normal Japanese breakfast. Why raw eggs are safe in Japan, how to eat TKG, and Ibaraki's egg story.

item.title: Nakaminato Fish Market: Ibaraki’s seafood street
item.description: A local's guide to Nakaminato Fish Market in Hitachinaka, Ibaraki: what to eat (kaisendon, sushi, monkfish), how to get there from Tokyo, and tips.

item.title: Hitachi Aki Soba: Ibaraki’s autumn noodles
item.description: Hitachi Aki Soba is Ibaraki's famous buckwheat from Hitachi-Ota. Why November is new soba season, and how to eat it: zaru, kenchin and tsuke soba.

item.title: I went to see the kochia!
item.description: The red kochia hill at Hitachi Seaside Park, Ibaraki, about 1 hour from Tokyo. When the color peaks, tips to avoid lines, and fun facts from a local.

item.title: Is Ibaraki really Japan's “least attractive” prefecture?
item.description: Ibaraki often ranks last in Japan's prefecture attractiveness survey. A local shows what people miss: blue flower hills, Fukuroda Falls, Oarai and more.

item.title: 5 things that surprise people about rural Japan
item.description: Life in rural Japan is not like Tokyo. Cars, vegetables from neighbors, quiet nights, strict garbage rules and the konbini, from a local in Ibaraki.

item.title: Overtime in Japan: what it's really like
item.description: Do Japanese people really work that much? An honest look at overtime culture in Japan, why people stay late, and what is changing, from a local worker.

item.title: Easy one-day trip to Ibaraki from Tokyo
item.description: An easy one-day trip to Ibaraki from Tokyo by train and bus: Hitachi Seaside Park, Nakaminato Fish Market and Oarai Isosaki Shrine, plus local tips.

item.title: Unwritten rules of the Japanese countryside
item.description: The unwritten rules of rural Japan nobody tells you: greetings, omiyage, the neighborhood association, returning favors and more, from a local in Ibaraki.

item.title: Hoshiimo season is here!
item.description: Hoshiimo is dried sweet potato, chewy and naturally sweet, and Ibaraki makes most of it in Japan. How it is made and where to buy it in winter.
